name: Kim Mun
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 3 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ratliff, Martha. 2010. Hmong-Mien language history. Pacific Linguistics 613. Canberra: Pacific Linguistics (open access, ANU Open Research); with Clark, Eddie R. 2008. A phonological analysis and comparison of two Kim Mun varieties in Laos and Vietnam. MA thesis, Payap University (open, the Internet Archive copy) as the first-hand phonology; Ratliff, Martha. 2007. Contrastive vowel length in Mienic: inheritance or diffusion? SEALS XIII, 223-229 (SEALang copy) as the fuller version of the same passage.
catalog_quote: 4) Two independent descriptions of Mien (Downer 1961, Purnell 1965) and a note on Mun in Shintani and Yang (1990) show these two vowel length languages are characterized by a prosody that alternates short and long (or light and heavy) syllables. Downer (1961:539) describes Mien (“Highland Yao”) as follows: “[Reduced syllables] are of two kinds—regular reduced syllables, and reduced syllables in -a. The two kinds agree in having weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words …”. Given the iambic rhythm of these languages, not only must non-phrase-final syllables be light, but phrase-final syllables (syntactic heads) must maintain a certain gravity. ... [p. 199, Hmong-Mien nominal prefixes:] They are unstressed, and in some languages they may harmonize with the nouns to which they are attached (Chen 1993).

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (310 pp, text). Printed p. 28 (p. 39): the passage is there as point "4)" of §2.1.3.2. Only difference: the compiler quote elides one sentence inside Downer's quotation with "..": the PDF reads "[Reduced syllables] are of two kinds—regular reduced syllables, and reduced syllables in -a. The two kinds agree in having weaker stress and shorter duration than the following full syllables so that a strong iambic rhythm is imparted to disyllabic words …". Fn. 18 (135 Shintani & Yang sentences, vowel length correlates with phrase-final position) is on the same page. p. 199 (p. 212), §4.2.1: "They are unstressed, and in some languages they may harmonize with…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Kim Mun is an 8-tone language; the only stress-like statement is second-hand: Mien and Mun share an iambic light-heavy prosody in which reduced/minor syllables and nominal prefixes are unstressed and short, and the following full (word/phrase-final) syllable carries the prominence and full tone. Clark 2008 (first-hand, Lao and Vietnam Kim Mun) never mentions stress but describes toneless mid-pitch minor syllables and non-final vowel shortening with tone neutralization, consistent with that picture.
new_statements.exceptions: None for Kim Mun; the direct 'weaker stress' wording is Downer's about Iu Mien (Highland Yao), extended to Mun by Ratliff on the strength of a note in Shintani & Yang 1990.
new_statements.domain_note: Ratliff frames it as word/phrase prosody: non-phrase-final syllables light, phrase-final syllables (syntactic heads) heavy; fn. 18 reports Hainan Mun vowel length correlating with phrase-final position. Clark 2008 pp. 83, 117 reports non-word-final vowel shortening and tone neutralization in citation-form compounds.
new_statements.identity_note: Clark 2008 describes 'Lao Kim Mun' (Lantien/Lanten of Luang Namtha, Laos) and 'Vietnam Kim Mun' (Lao Cai); Ratliff's second-hand note concerns Hainan Mun (Shintani & Yang 1990). All fall under kimm1245 (Glottolog lists no dialect children). Downer 1961 and Purnell 1965, quoted by Ratliff, describe Iu Mien (iumi1238), not Kim Mun.

tone_statements.quote: Mun tonal systems vary. E.Mun has only five tones in unchecked syllables, whereas W.Mun has seven tones. The *A1 and *C1 tones in E.Mun have each split into two tone depending on the initial: *A1 > 33 (A1.1) and 45 (A1.2), and *C1 > 11 (C1.1) and 31 (C1.2). Also the *D1 and D2 have split, depending on the final: *D1 > 45 (D1.1) and 33’/45 (D1.2) and *D2 > 21 (D2.1) and 31’ (D2.2). (See details in 2.2) In addition, *A2 and *C2 have merged, and there are also partial mergers of *D1 with *A1 (D1.1 with A1.2), of *D2 (D2.2) with *A2, and of *C1 (C1.1) with *B2, as shown in figure 6.
tone_statements.locator: p. 172, §2.1 Tones, above Figure 6 'Eastern Mun tones'
tone_statements.summary: E.Mun (Jinxiu) 5 unchecked tones, W.Mun (Baise) 7; high-series splits by initial; checked tones split by final; Chao values given.

sources.citation: Clark, Eddie R. 2008. A phonological analysis and comparison of two Kim Mun varieties in Laos and Vietnam. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. 223 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: not located online or in the libraries checked
sources.note: Silent on stress: the words 'stress'/'accent' do not occur anywhere in the thesis. Both varieties have 8 tones (5.1.3, 6.1.3); word structure (C.)C1(C2)V(C3)T with optional word-initial minor (pre-)syllable that has 'no distinctive tone', a shortened schwa, and 'pitch level.. of about mid range' (p. 91; Vietnam variety 'do not carry tone', p. 125); non-word-final syllables show vowel shortening and Shintani-style 'tone neutralization where only the target pitch level is produced' (p. 83; p. 117).

sources.note: §2.1 Tones (pp. 170-173) and §2.2 Tone correspondences (pp. 173 ff.): Proto-Mjuenic *A *B *C *D split into 8 categories by initial voicing; Eastern Mun (Jinxiu) has 5 tones in unchecked syllables (high 33/13/11/45, low 31/11/31/21, with *A2=*C2 merger), Western Mun (Baise) 7, each high-series tone (*A1 *B1 *C1 *D1) having split in two conditioned by the initial type (e.g. *A1 > 354 vs 13, *B1 > 45 vs 35); checked *D tones split by final; p. 168 contrasts E.Mun 5 vs W.Mun 7 tones; tone-value tables figs. 6-8.
